title: Researchers Cut Quantum Computing Costs With New Scheduler
excerpt: Cutting large quantum computations into smaller pieces can actually *increase* overall processing time, until now. A new scheduler demonstrably reverses this trend, reducing peak (P90) latency by up to 39% through intelligent distribution across multiple processors. Reconstruction costs alone account for over 83% of the performance hit from cutting circuits, highlighting the need for holistic resource management.
content:
A reduction in processing time of up to thirty-nine percent has been achieved through a new approach to distributing quantum computations across multiple processors. A resource-aware scheduler intelligently decides whether to run circuits whole, cut them for single processor execution or distribute them amongst several QPUs, quantum processing units. This scheduling system manages complex calculations across multiple quantum computers; it can run circuits completely, in sections on one computer or spread amongst several.

This approach accounts for the time taken to move data between processors *and* reassemble results, factors that typically cause delays when tasks are split. By optimising this process, speed improvements were achieved over dividing circuits without considering these elements.

The University of Minnesota team has developed a new approach to tackling increasingly complex quantum calculations that often exceed the capacity of individual quantum processing units (QPUs). Their research focuses on intelligently managing these computations across multiple QPUs; rather than simply dividing circuits into smaller pieces, akin to splitting chapters amongst writers for a book, the scheduler considers whether to run them whole, sequentially on one processor or distribute them amongst several.

Moving data between processors and reassembling results can sharply delay execution because it is key. Optimising this process yielded reductions in processing time of up to thirty-nine percent compared with naive circuit division methods. The system measures P90 latency, essentially how long 90% of jobs take to complete, like measuring checkout times at a store, and seeks ways to minimise it. But will this resource-aware scheduling prove effective enough to unlock truly scalable quantum computation.

Novel quantum circuit scheduling minimizes latency via intelligent distribution

Up to thirty-nine percent reduction in P90 latency, the completion time for ninety percent of jobs, is now possible with distributed execution compared to single quantum processing units (QPUs). This improvement was previously unattainable due to limitations in hardware capacity. At University of Minnesota, researchers achieved these gains by intelligently deciding how best to execute complex calculations: running them intact, dividing sequentially across one QPU, or distributing amongst several. Their system specifically accounts for communication delays between processors and reconstruction, a process that typically constitutes over eighty-three percent of overhead when splitting circuits.

Scheduling overhead never exceeded 0.038% of total job completion time during experiments. Explicitly modelling communication costs alongside circuit ‘reconstruction’ accounted for the majority, over eighty-three percent, of extra work created when splitting calculations. The system also uses hardware timing derived from simulated quantum processing units (QPUs) and AerSimulator noise models to accurately predict performance; this allows informed decisions about resource allocation. This predictive capability is key to minimising latency in distributed systems.

Simulation limitations necessitate validation with physical quantum processors

The scheduler demonstrably improves performance by treating distributed quantum computing as a runtime challenge, not simply partitioning circuits. However, evaluation relies heavily upon simulations of QPUs, an inherent limitation given that real-world hardware invariably introduces variations not fully captured by modelling alone. Competing approaches focused on optimising circuit division and reconstruction techniques may still hold merit for specific workloads or QPU architectures. Real-world quantum hardware’s notorious variability potentially impacts performance beyond what models can predict; therefore reliance upon simulation does introduce some uncertainty. Nevertheless, effective distributed quantum computing requires holistic runtime management; dividing circuits is insufficient to achieve significant gains.

This research demonstrated a resource-aware scheduler for distributed quantum computing (DQC) capable of intelligently selecting the most efficient execution plan, intact, sequential, or distributed, based on real-time modeling of both quantum processing unit (QPU) operation and classical communication/reconstruction costs. The study found that reconstruction accounts for over eighty-three percent of overhead when splitting circuits, while distributing calculations reduced latency by up to thirty-nine percent compared to single-QPU execution. These results indicate DQC benefits from being treated as a runtime scheduling problem encompassing all resources, rather than solely focusing on circuit partitioning.
